stances.claim: Both the Constitution and the Bible ordain the separation of Church and state -- the constitutional wall is 'inviolable' and the biblical command is 'render unto Caesar.'
The state is neutral among religious denominations and may not fund exclusive religious infrastructure, subsidize dogmas, pay clergy for strictly religious duties, or condemn beliefs.
The Church's general policy -- based partly on the 'render unto Caesar' command -- is to avoid confronting the state on political issues and to intervene only on matters of faith and morals.

stances.claim: The 'stupid God' confrontation will escalate and needlessly divide the nation unless handled properly -- Cardinal Tagle's call for calm and not being 'distracted' is the right response.
stances.rhetorical_move: de-escalation endorsement grounded in named Church authority

stances.claim: Crossing the wall of separation to find what unites -- build roads, create jobs, feed the hungry, help the poor -- is the constructive alternative to the 'kill, kill, kill' of poor addicts and loiterers.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban takes up the constitutional and biblical foundations of church-state separation amid the controversy over President Duterte's 'stupid God' remark. The 1987 Constitution's Preamble recognizes the 'elevating influence of religion' (Aglipay v. Ruiz, March 13, 1937) but Article II, Section 6 mandates an 'inviolable' wall of separation, reinforced by the Bill of Rights' non-establishment clause -- meaning the state cannot fund exclusive religious infrastructure, subsidize dogmas, pay clergy for strictly religious duties, or condemn beliefs. Scripturally, the Lord's 'Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's' (Matthew 22 / Mark 12) establishes the same divide. Drawing on his unique credential as the only Filipino appointed by Saint Pope John Paul II to the Vatican-based Pontifical Council for the Laity (1996-2002), the author explains that the Church's general policy is to avoid confronting the state on political issues and to intervene only on matters of faith and morals -- though it faced a painful dilemma during the 2001 EDSA Revolution that nearly split the Catholic hierarchy (details deferred to another column). Against this backdrop, he endorses Cardinal Tagle's call to 'be calm' and not be 'distracted' by the 'stupid God' confrontation, warning it will needlessly divide the nation. He closes with a triple-refrain rallying cry: crossing the wall to find what unites -- 'build, build, build' roads; 'jobs, jobs, jobs' for the unemployed; 'food, food, food' for the hungry; 'help, help, help' the poor -- while abandoning the 'kill, kill, kill' of poor addicts and loiterers in favor of chasing the rich drug lords, and ending the 'curse, curse, curse' of God, Allah, and Yahweh.
